(b)(i) | Expected real rate of return = 4.5% – 4.5% = 0% (1)
Actual real rate of return = 4% – (–1%) = 5% (1)
(b)(ii) Gain, because (1)
the actual real rate of return is higher than the expected real rate of return. (1)

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
(c) According to the quantity theory of money, explain how the increase in money supply affects the general
price level in the long run. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
(c) QTM: MV = PY, where M = money stock, V = velocity of circulation of money, P = general price level and Y
= real output (1)
Assuming Y is constant in long run, (1)
an increase in M will result in a rise in P by the same percentage. (2)

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
(d) Based on the quantity theory of money, predict the effect of increasing the money supply on the price level.
State the assumption(s) needed to reach your conclusion. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
(d) - QTM: MV = PY, where M = money stock, V = velocity of circulation of money, P = general price level and
Y = real output, assuming V constant. (2)
- An increase in M leads to an increase in P when Y increases by a smaller proportion. (2)
OR
- An increase in M leads to an increase in P by the same percentage when Y is constant. (2)
max: 2

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
(b) Based on the quantity theory of money, predict the effect of an open market purchase of government bonds
by the central bank on the price level. State the assumption(s) needed to reach your conclusion. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
(b) MV = PY, where M: money supply, V: velocity of circulation of money, P: price level, and Y: output
Assume V and Y are both constant. Then when M increases, P would increase by the same proportion.
OR
Assume V is constant. Then when the percentage increase in M is higher than that in Y, P would increase as
well.
(4)

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
(c) 'The continuous open market purchase of government bonds by the central bank is the cause of inflation in
the economy.' Justify the statement with reference to the classical quantity theory of money. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
(c) MV = PY, where M: money supply, V: velocity of circulation of money, P: price level and Y: output
Assume V and Y being constant. (2)
A continuous increase in M (caused by the open market purchase) would result in a continuous increase in P,
i.e. inflation. (2)

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
(a) ‘Deflation will occur if the amount of goods and services produced is growing faster than money supply.’
Explain this statement in terms of the quantity theory of money. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
(a) QTM: MV = PY, where
M = money supply,
V = velocity of circulation of money, assumed to be constant,
P = price level, and
Y = real output.
% increase in Y being larger than % increase in M would result in a drop in P, i.e. deflation occurs.
(4)

questions.solution:
(d) In Country A with a lower GDP:
- its per capita GDP may be higher (it has a much smaller population) and more likely to live a better life
there
- its income may be more evenly distributed ⇒ more attractive to the very low income people of Country
B
- its GDP may have a very different composition, e.g. a much larger component of consumption
expenditure ⇒ more attractive to people who prefer to enjoy life immediately
- its real GDP may be higher: it has a much lower price level
- its GDP is very much underestimated / Country B's GDP is very much overestimated (illustrate with an
appropriate example)

[Mark the FIRST TWO points only.]

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
(c) Suppose after trade, Country B has a higher consumption level of both clothing and rice than Country A.
Give THREE reasons to explain why we cannot conclude that people in Country B generally enjoy a
higher living standard as compared to Country A. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
(c) This is because we do not know:
- the population size / per capita income of both countries. If B's population size is three times, say, as that
of A, then in general B's living standard is not higher than A.
- the income distribution of both countries. If B's income is highly unevenly distributed but A's is not, then
we cannot conclude that.
- other social costs of both countries. e.g. if B has a higher crime rate / more pollution / more serious social
instability / etc., then B's living standard may not be generally higher than A.
- other social benefits of both countries. e.g. if B has less social benefits / fewer leisure hours / etc., then B's
living standard may not be generally higher than A.
- what other goods besides rice and clothing these two countries have. e.g. if B has less other goods, then
the conclusion may be wrong.
- any other relevant point
[Mark the FIRST THREE points only.]
@2; max: 6

questions.solution:
- income distribution: If income is unevenly distributed, the living standard of ordinary people will be
overestimated.
- composition of output: If a large proportion of total output consists of capital goods, national defense, etc.,
the living standard will be overestimated.
- undesirable effects of production: The problems of pollution or traffic congestion would lower the living
standard. Therefore, the living standard would be overestimated without such information.
- amount of leisure: Leisure would raise the living standard. Therefore, the living standard would be
underestimated without such information.
- unreported production activities: The consumption of non-marketed goods / the existence of unreported
transactions would improve the living standard. Therefore, the living standard would be underestimated
without such information.

in the composition of output)
- There are more problems of pollution or traffic congestion in country X (different undesirable effects of
production)
- The people of country X enjoy less leisure (different amount of leisure)

unreported production activities)

standard. Therefore, the corresponding change in the general living standard would be overestimated
without such information.

general living standard would be underestimated without such information.
- unreported production activities: The consumption of non-marketed goods / the existence of unreported
transactions would improve the living standard. Therefore, the corresponding change in the general living
standard would be underestimated without such information.

the economy principle.

would be just as certain as the old.
Convenience: There is no change in the method of tax collection, so the change in tax system would have no
effect on convenience.

'The above change in labour force necessarily implies a rise in the unemployment rate in 2021 in Hong Kong'. Do you
agree? Explain your answer. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
No. Unemployment rate = (unemployed population / labour force) × 100%. (2)
Despite the decrease in the size of HK's labour force, the unemployment rate would fall (or remain
unchanged) if the percentage decrease in the unemployed population was greater than (or equal to) that in the
labour force. (2)

questions.subject: Macro
questions.text:
Since the 2010s, the government of Saudi Arabia has been actively promoting football development.
(b) Suppose some unemployed youngsters stopped seeking jobs and enrolled in the full-time training
programmes of these football academies. Explain how the unemployment rate in Saudi Arabia would be
affected. (4 marks)
questions.solution:
(b) Unemployment rate = (unemployed population / labour force) × 100%. As some unemployed young adults
enrol in the full-time training programmes of those football academies, the number of unemployed and the
labour force would decrease by the same magnitude. The percentage decrease in the unemployed population
would be bigger than that in the labour force. As a result, the unemployment rate decreases. (4)

(b) Losses to society caused by unemployment:
